children: The Sebi proposals do not yet address why CAS volumes have stayed thin since launch, and that has a specific, mechanical cause, says expert

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) is considering changes to the newly introduced closing auction session (CAS), as early market experience points to concerns around liquidity, price discovery and the interaction between the cash and derivatives markets.

The regulator has proposed two alternative trading schedules for CAS and equity derivatives, alongside changes to the methodology used to calculate derivatives settlement prices. The proposals come less than two months after the closing auction mechanism was introduced on 03 August, signalling an early attempt to calibrate the framework based on how it is functioning in live markets.

Closing auctions are widely used by global exchanges to establish a representative closing price by concentrating orders into a defined period. When supported by sufficient participation and liquidity, the mechanism can improve price discovery and reduce execution costs.

“Closing auctions are a well-established mechanism globally and, when backed by adequate participation and liquidity, can lower execution costs and improve the quality of closing-price discovery. Evidence from markets such as Paris and Italy supports this,” said Narinder Wadhwa, MD & CEO, SKI Capital Services.

India’s move to CAS is therefore directionally sound; the experience since its introduction on August 3 suggests that the mechanism now needs some calibration as market participants become accustomed to it, he added.
Sebi Weighs Two Trading Windows

Under Option A proposed by Sebi, continuous trading in stocks covered by CAS would continue until 3.30 p.m., followed by a 10-minute closing auction from 3.31 p.m. to 3.40 p.m. Equity derivatives trading would continue until 3.45 p.m.

Option B would end continuous trading in CAS stocks at 3.15 p.m., followed by the auction between 3.15 p.m. and 3.25 p.m. The futures and options segment would retain its existing 3.30 p.m. closing time.

Wadhwa said Option A appears more workable from a market-liquidity perspective as it preserves the existing continuous trading session. “It avoids having CAS stocks stop continuous trading at 3.15 p.m. while non-CAS stocks continue to trade until 3.30 p.m.,” he said.

The timing proposals form part of Sebi’s broader review of the closing auction mechanism and derivatives settlement methodology. The regulator had earlier indicated that it would review the settlement-price mechanism following the introduction of CAS.
Settlement Prices In Focus

Sebi has proposed two alternatives for calculating settlement prices for equity derivatives. Under the first, trades executed during both the continuous trading session (CTS) and CAS would be used to determine settlement prices. Under the second, settlement prices would initially continue to be calculated using CTS trades alone, with CAS trades potentially being incorporated after at least one year.
The issue assumes greater significance on expiry days, when concentrated activity around the close can influence both cash-market prices and derivatives settlement.

“Bringing CAS trades into the settlement-price calculation should make the reference price more representative of actual market activity and strengthen the link between the cash and derivatives markets,” said Kamlesh Shroff, President, ANMI.
“It should also help reduce the impact of any sharp movement concentrated around the closing auction, particularly on expiry days,” he added.

Sebi has also proposed shortening the transition period between continuous trading and CAS to one minute from five minutes. The post-auction trading window for equity derivatives would be reduced to five minutes from the existing 10 minutes.
Restrictions On CAS Orders

The consultation paper also proposes changes to the information and order types available during the closing auction. Exchanges would not display an indicative index value based on the indicative equilibrium price during CAS.

“Removing the indicative index value during CAS could reduce speculative trading based on an evolving, non-traded index level. However, it may also reduce visibility into the broader market’s indicative direction,” said Dhirender Singh Bisht, AVP, Equity Research, SMC Global Securities.

Sebi has proposed restricting the cancellation of certain orders during the auction. Limit orders placed within 1 per cent either side of the reference price would not be allowed to be cancelled, although investors would be permitted to modify them to improve the price. Unexecuted iceberg orders would also enter the auction as regular, fully disclosed limit orders.
Is Thin Liquidity The Bigger Problem?
While the proposed changes address several operational aspects of CAS, some market participants believe the more fundamental issue is the lack of liquidity during the auction itself.

“The proposals do not yet address why CAS volumes have stayed thin since launch, and that has a specific, mechanical cause,” said Sarvam Goel, Founder, Pocketful. According to Goel, the structure of a single-price auction makes conventional market-making difficult because market makers cannot capture the bid-ask spread in the same way they can during continuous trading.

“A market maker earns from the bid-ask spread, and a single-price auction removes that spread entirely, so there is no economic incentive to quote continuously through the window,” he said. Goel said the result could be a greater concentration of speculative or directional orders during the auction, potentially contributing to sharp price movements around the closing mechanism.
The contrasting views highlight the broader challenge facing Sebi— improving closing-price discovery without compromising liquidity or creating unintended incentives for market participants.

Sebi has invited public comments on the consultation paper until 03 October 2026. The proposed changes will determine how the closing auction mechanism evolves as the regulator seeks to balance representative price discovery with liquidity and the functioning of the wider cash and derivatives markets.
